rival_mechanisms.name: Guard-cell starch/hexose DEPLETION at dawn (opposite sign to the hypothesis)
rival_mechanisms.why_it_could_produce_the_same_observatio: Blocking dawn starch-to-glucose conversion in Arabidopsis leaves guard cells with almost no glucose and adds 40 min to the stomatal opening time constant. Any previous-day treatment that lowers dawn guard-cell glucose therefore produces reduced morning opening. This is the same observation as the hypothesis predicts but with the hexose term reversed in sign.

rival_mechanisms.name: Osmotic (non-signalling) inhibition by high solute load
rival_mechanisms.why_it_could_produce_the_same_observatio: Mannitol, a non-metabolisable osmoticum, reproduces the stomatal inhibition seen with 100 mM sucrose, and a model reduces gs simply as leaf osmotic potential becomes more negative with carbohydrate accumulation. Elevated leaf solutes after a cool night could therefore lower morning gs osmotically, with no hexose sensing involved.

rival_mechanisms.name: Circadian gating and predawn conductance priming
rival_mechanisms.why_it_could_produce_the_same_observatio: Nocturnal conductance is clock-driven, persists under constant conditions, correlates positively with relative growth rate, and is proposed to prime stomata for early daylight. A cool night that suppresses growth would lower nocturnal and predawn conductance, so stomata start the morning from a lower aperture regardless of leaf sugar status.

rival_mechanisms.name: Morning transient: stomatal opening kinetics rather than steady state
rival_mechanisms.why_it_could_produce_the_same_observatio: Stomatal responses to light and temperature are slower than photosynthetic responses, and measured opening time constants shift by tens of minutes. Morning gs sampled at a fixed clock time is an unfinished transient, so any previous-day effect on opening kinetics reads as reduced morning conductance without changing the eventual steady state.

rival_mechanisms.name: Direct depression of next-day photosynthetic capacity by low night temperature
rival_mechanisms.why_it_could_produce_the_same_observatio: A validated crop model reduces next-day leaf photosynthesis when night minimum temperature falls below about 10-15 C, citing measured tomato reductions. Lower next-day assimilation raises intercellular CO2 and, through A-gs coupling, lowers morning conductance. The cause is photosynthetic carry-over, not a hexose signal.

rival_mechanisms.name: Morning VPD / leaf-to-air gradient and low-irradiance conditions
rival_mechanisms.why_it_could_produce_the_same_observatio: Dawn conductance maxima are attributed predominantly to low morning VPD, and standard stomatal models systematically overestimate morning gs below 0.6 kPa VPD and below 500 umol m-2 s-1 irradiance. A cool night changes dawn air temperature, humidity and dew, so 'otherwise-equivalent clear days' are not equivalent in the morning boundary layer, and reduced morning gs versus expectation is already a documented artefact.

rival_mechanisms.name: ABA and cold-stress signalling carried over from the cool night
rival_mechanisms.why_it_could_produce_the_same_observatio: Low temperature increases ABA in cucumber roots and leaves. ABA is the canonical closing signal, and the corpus's own hexose-closure mechanism is itself described as ABA-mediated, so cold-induced ABA and hexose signalling converge on the same effector and are not separable from a morning gs measurement.

rival_mechanisms.name: Whole-plant carbon economics / low sink demand (not guard-cell sensing)
rival_mechanisms.why_it_could_produce_the_same_observatio: Optimization theory predicts that when marginal demand for non-structural carbohydrate is low, stomata should close to favour growth over photosynthesis. A cool night suppresses sink demand, so this predicts reduced morning opening from whole-plant economics rather than guard-cell hexose. Note the same paper reports that this theory class fails to explain nocturnal stomatal opening.

rival_mechanisms.name: Cold-induced anatomical and developmental change (stomatal density, leaf thickness)
rival_mechanisms.why_it_could_produce_the_same_observatio: Cold-developed Arabidopsis leaves were twice as thick and had higher epidermal and stomatal cell densities. Repeated cool nights change the stomatal population and diffusion path, altering conductance structurally, on a developmental rather than an overnight timescale.

rival_mechanisms.name: Low root-zone temperature reducing root hydraulic conductivity / aquaporin gating
rival_mechanisms.why_it_could_produce_the_same_observatio: Cold roots would limit morning water supply and force stomatal closure. One corpus model implements temperature-dependent hydraulic conductances that limit stomatal opening under cold weather, and a root-hydraulics review supplies the conductance-to-water-potential link. However the assigned root-hydraulics paper 1209 contains no occurrence of 'temperature' at all, and the primary aquaporin/low-root-temperature studies appear in this corpus only as reference-list citations, so the classic rival is under-evidenced here despite being physiologically plausible.

rival_mechanisms.name: Incomplete overnight rehydration / predawn leaf water potential recovery
rival_mechanisms.why_it_could_produce_the_same_observatio: A cool night could slow rehydration and leave a lower predawn leaf water potential, limiting morning opening. Searches for overnight rehydration and predawn recovery returned only drought-context and methodological statements (predawn disequilibrium with soil water potential, nocturnal transpiration delaying rehydration under warm nights), none linking cool nights to next-morning conductance. No claim is emitted.

rival_mechanisms.name: Photosynthetic induction state as the limiting step in the morning
rival_mechanisms.why_it_could_produce_the_same_observatio: Morning assimilation is induction-limited and stomatal limitation during induction is explicitly quantified in the corpus, so morning gs tracks induction state. Corpus material on induction is measured against CO2, leaf temperature and VPD treatments, not against previous-night temperature, so the specific carry-over link is not evidenced.

notes:
PROSECUTION SUMMARY. Every span was pinned with a whitespace-mapping matcher and re-read from
disk; char_start/char_end/verbatim_text are byte-identical to text.md and text_hash is sha256 of
the raw slice. 30 claims from 15 documents. No quote, offset, hash, number, species or citation
was invented; two candidate spans initially failed to pin (1060 because the raw text contains a
control character in "10 \u0002C", 146 because of sentence-initial capitalisation) and were
re-pinned with corrected phrases rather than guessed.

DECISIVE COUNTER TO C1/C4. 438 (Arabidopsis, direct measurement): blocking guard-cell starch
degradation leaves guard cells with almost undetectable glucose and INCREASES the opening time
constant by 40 min; the authors conclude dawn starch degradation is "required to maintain the
cytoplasmic sugar pool, clearly needed for fast stomatal opening". Dawn guard-cell hexose is a
positive requirement for rapid morning opening, so the hypothesis assigns the wrong sign to C1
in exactly the compartment and timescale it needs.

DOSE AND PHASE BOUNDARY ON THE SUGAR-CLOSURE EFFECT. Where sugars do close stomata, the corpus
scopes it to (a) high concentrations (432: low concentrations had little or no effect), (b)
periods of high photosynthetic rate / carbon saturation (507, 1106, 236), and (c) apoplastic
sucrose sensed by hexokinase with ABA as the effector (432, 507). 236 further shows 100 mM
MANNITOL reproduces the inhibition, so the high-sugar effect is at least partly osmotic rather
than hexose-specific. A residual dawn hexose pool is in the low-concentration, carbon-depleted
regime where the corpus reports promotion or no effect.

IDENTIFIABILITY. At least four rivals predict an observationally IDENTICAL morning-gs pattern
after a cool night: reduced circadian/predawn priming (023, 1187), low sink demand under carbon
economics (090), cold-depressed next-day photosynthetic capacity with A-gs coupling (1060), and
cold-induced ABA (012, 432). 046 makes this worse: in the only corpus model coupling temperature,
carbohydrate and dawn gs, cold temperatures with LOW NSC produce LARGER morning conductance and
dawn gs is attributed predominantly to low morning VPD. The hypothesis is therefore not
identifiable from morning gs on "otherwise-equivalent clear days" alone; discrimination requires
paired dawn guard-cell (not whole-leaf) hexose assay, ABA measurement, predawn water potential,
gn/predawn gs, and full opening-kinetics time courses rather than a single morning reading.

COUNTER TO C3's MECHANISM. 146 (Arabidopsis, direct measurement) attributes cold sugar
accumulation to increased abundance and activity of SYNTHETIC enzymes, not to failed conversion
into structural carbohydrate, and reports that glucose specifically DECLINES steadily from 4 d of
cold while fructose, sucrose and total sugars do not change. Elevated hexose is therefore neither
mechanistically as assumed nor durable.

HONEST SUPPORT FOUND. 090 states that progressive stomatal opening as NSC stores are depleted by
nocturnal growth could explain nocturnal opening, which matches the hypothesis's logic; it is
speculative theory at the whole-plant NSC level, and 046 reports that this theory class cannot
currently explain nocturnal stomatal opening without corrective fitness factors. 073 reproduces
the hypothesised sign but via leaf osmotic potential, not hexose signalling.

SEARCHED FOR AND NOT FOUND IN CORPUS. (1) Any direct measurement linking previous-night
temperature to next-morning stomatal conductance. (2) Any measurement of dawn guard-cell or leaf
hexose paired with morning gs on clear days. (3) Any in-body statement that low root-zone
temperature reduces root hydraulic conductivity: 1209 contains no occurrence of "temperature",
and Murai-Hatano 2008, Lee 2012 (PIP2;5), Wan 2001 and Kuwagata 2012 appear only in reference
lists of 031, 046, 012, 457 and 783. (4) Any cool-night to incomplete-overnight-rehydration to
morning-gs chain. (5) Starting paper 012 (cucumber cold tolerance) contains ZERO in-body
occurrences of "stomatal", so it cannot support any stomatal link. Absence in this corpus is
absence of evidence, not proof of absence.
